newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Fresh shooting at nightfall in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fresh shooting at nightfall in Brazzaville.

text.p: Fresh shooting rocked the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Monday amid confusion over the timing of a new truce to which President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso have put their names.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who helped negotiate the truce proposed by Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, said on Sunday it would start at midnight (2300 GMT) on Monday.

"There was some sporadic shooting during the day, but until the shelling started it has been relatively calm compared to recent days," said an aid worker returning from Brazzaville to the Democratic Republic of the Congo capital Kinshasa.
The sound of mortar and heavy machinegun fire could be heard across the Congo River in Kinshasa after nightfall.
One source close to the mediators said in Brazzaville during a Monday morning lull that the guns fell silent on instructions.

A mediation committee under Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas was meeting earlier on Monday. "I understand that the military commanders are going to attempt to find ways of applying the ceasefire today," the source said.
Lissouba and Sassou initialled a ceasefire on Saturday to halt over a month of bloody political and ethnic clashes.

The bloody showdown in the capital of the oil-producing former French colony began on June 5 when soldiers surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of a now-postponed July 27 presidential election.
The clashes and indiscriminate shellfire have killed hundreds of people, many of them civilians, medical workers say.
Lissouba's spokesman Gregoire Lefouba had said the truce would begin at midnight on Sunday.

Sahnoun told BBC radio on Sunday that talks would take place in Gabon's capital Libreville by Tuesday or Wednesday on national reconciliation and creating an environment for elections some time over the next two months.
Plans are taking shape for a U.N.-sponsored, mainly African peacekeeping force.

Relief workers are keen to provide neighbourhoods deprived of clean water and electricity with emergency sanitation, particularly in the north, Sassou's stronghold. Food shortages are also a problem, they say.
"The central water supply system to the north of Brazzaville has been damaged and electricity has also been partly cut off to the north," UNICEF Kinshasa spokeswoman Danielle Maillefer said.
UNICEF says measles have killed 10 people.
Lissouba's mandate expires at the end of August. He says the constitution allows a 90-day extension to organise elections. Sassou demands a national salvation government.
Lissouba, Sassou and Kolelas, whose militia has kept out of the latest fighting, planned to contest the July 27 election.
Kolelas's militia was at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election.
